items.claim: Uploading a file with an executable extension is only remote code execution when the stored file is reachable through the web server and executed in a context the server interprets, so storage outside the document root defeats the finding regardless of the extension.
items.disproof: It IS RCE when the stored file sits under a served path and a request to it returns the body with an execution-interpreted content type, or when an include or deserialisation step reaches it; it is NOT RCE when retrieval requires a filesystem path the web server does not expose, which is exactly the case a report must prove rather than assume.

items.body: Mechanism: Uploading a file with an executable extension is only remote code execution when the stored file is reachable through the web server and executed in a context the server interprets, so storage outside the document root defeats the finding regardless of the extension. How to apply it in the field: treat this as the fp_rule it is — a hunter must be able to state the concrete observation that demonstrates it, with a request and response in hand, before the finding is reportable. Boundary of the rule: It IS RCE when the stored file sits under a served path and a request to it returns the body with an execution-interpreted content type, or when an include or deserialisation step reaches it; it is NOT RCE when retrieval requires a filesystem path the web server does not expose, which is exactly the case a report must prove rather than assume.

items.claim: The convincing upload evidence is a request/response pair showing the uploaded content served back over HTTP from the stored location, which is what distinguishes a stored upload from a file that merely landed on disk.
items.disproof: If no HTTP GET returns the stored bytes, the upload may still be a real defect when the content is later parsed as an archive, deserialised, or served from a different application sharing the disk; but when the file is never served and never opened by a parser, the absence of retrieval evidence means the report must state an unproven execution path rather than claiming RCE.

items.claim: Trusting the MIME value supplied with the upload request as proof of file type is a false negative, because that value is chosen by the client and can be set to anything regardless of the actual bytes.
items.disproof: It IS adequate when the type is determined from the file content by the server rather than taken from the request; it is NOT adequate when the decision reads the client-declared value, since the attacker controls that field directly and the same request can be replayed with any declared type.

items.claim: An extension or MIME allowlist is defeated when the attacker controls the stored filename the application later uses in a server-side include, an archive extraction, or an image re-encode step, because the check ran on one representation while the interpreter acts on another.
items.disproof: It is not a bypass when the stored name is generated server-side from the content rather than from the request, so the attacker never chooses the suffix the interpreter sees; it is a bypass when a request-controlled name or a container-within-container survives into the path that a parser acts on.

items.claim: The mere presence of an upload endpoint that accepts and stores a file is not a finding; what makes it reportable is a missing control on one specific dimension, such as execution on retrieval, unlimited size, or attacker-chosen storage name.
items.disproof: It IS reportable when any of those dimensions is missing and demonstrated; it is NOT a finding when the upload is size-limited, stored under a server-generated name outside the web root, and never passed to an interpreter, since a stored file with no reachable handler is expected application behaviour.
